narrative:
The model predicts you have a 22% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The decision rests mainly on three aspects of your profile. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this is the same as the average for students who passed, in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees it as increasing your risk. Next, your very low weekly study time (under 2 hours) pushes the prediction toward failure; most students who passed dedicate 2–5 hours or more. Finally, the fact that you did not attend nursery school also contributes to the failing prediction, even though many successful students did attend one.

These three elements together outweigh the positive signals in your record, such as wanting to pursue higher education, having a stable family, and low absences. Because the combination points to a noticeable risk of not passing, the school has decided you must take extra courses.

To improve, focus first on building a consistent study routine of at least two hours most days. Consider structured support for subjects you find difficult, and talk with your teachers about whether revisiting foundational skills from earlier years could help close any gaps. Small, steady changes in study habits can meaningfully raise your chances of success.
